explanation:
## `&[T]` rather than `&Vec<T>`

```rust
fn sum(xs: &[i64]) -> i64
```

This one function is called four times in the solution - on the whole vector, on
each half, and on the first window - because all four are slices of the same
buffer. Had it been declared `&Vec<i64>`, only the first call would compile.

A `&Vec<T>` coerces to `&[T]` automatically through `Deref`, so writing the
slice type costs callers nothing and gains the function every array, every
slice, and every sub-range. The rule of thumb:

| Take | When |
| --- | --- |
| `&[T]` | you read a sequence |
| `&mut [T]` | you modify elements in place but never resize |
| `&Vec<T>` | almost never - only if you genuinely need `Vec`'s own methods |
| `Vec<T>` | you need to own it, resize it, or keep it |

The same applies to strings: `&str` reads, `String` owns. Taking `&String` is
the same mistake as taking `&Vec<T>`.

## A slice is a pointer and a length

```
v: Vec<i64>      ptr -> [ 1 ][ 2 ][ 3 ][ 4 ][ 5 ]   len 5   cap 8
&v[1..4]         ptr ------^                        len 3
```

Sixteen bytes on a 64-bit platform, and making one copies no elements. `split_at`
produces two of them pointing into the same buffer, which is sound precisely
because they are **non-overlapping** - and that matters when the mutable version
is involved:

```rust
let (a, b) = v.split_at_mut(mid);     // two &mut slices at once
```

This is the one sanctioned way to hold two exclusive references into one
collection. It is allowed because the function's signature guarantees the two
ranges are disjoint, so neither can observe the other's writes. There is no way
to express that with plain indexing, which is why `split_at_mut` is in the
standard library rather than something you write.

## The sliding window

```rust
let mut running = sum(&xs[0..k]);
for i in 1..=(xs.len() - k) {
    running = running - xs[i - 1] + xs[i + k - 1];
    ...
}
```

Each step removes the element that just left the window and adds the one that
just entered, so the whole scan is O(n) rather than O(n*k). For n = 2000 and
k = 1000 that is 2000 operations instead of two million.

The index arithmetic is the part to be careful about. In the body, `i >= 1` is
guaranteed by the loop's start, so `i - 1` cannot underflow; and
`i + k - 1 <= len - 1` because `i <= len - k`. Both are safe **because of the
guard above**:

```rust
if k == 0 || k > xs.len() { return None; }
```

Without it, `xs.len() - k` is a `usize` subtraction that goes negative - which
in Rust means:

```
thread 'main' panicked at 'attempt to subtract with overflow'
```

in a debug build, and wraps to roughly 1.8 x 10^19 in a release build, producing
a loop that runs effectively forever and indexes out of bounds on its first
iteration.

That difference is worth internalising. Rust's unsigned underflow is *checked* in
debug and *wrapping* in release - both defined, neither silent in the way C++'s
is, and still a bug either way. The guard is the fix; `checked_sub` is the
alternative when the subtraction is genuinely conditional:

```rust
let last_start = xs.len().checked_sub(k)?;      // None if k > len
```

## Ties resolve by the loop, not by a comparison

```rust
if running > best { best = running; at = i; }
```

Strictly greater, scanning left to right, so the first window achieving the
maximum is kept. That is the same trick as the word-count tie-break: the
required ordering came from the direction of the loop rather than from extra
logic. `>=` would report the last tied window instead, and the hidden case
`1 1 1 1` with `k = 2` is there to catch it.

## `Option<(usize, i64)>` instead of sentinels

```rust
fn best_window(xs: &[i64], k: usize) -> Option<(usize, i64)>
```

Two problems solved at once. There is no "no answer" index to invent - no `-1`,
no `usize::MAX` - and the index and the sum travel together so they cannot be
read in the wrong order or used independently.

The caller has to deal with it:

```rust
match best_window(&v, k) {
    Some((at, s)) => writeln!(out, "window {} {}", at, s),
    None          => writeln!(out, "window none"),
}
```

and that is the point. The `None` arm is not optional - leave it out and the
match is not exhaustive and the program does not compile. Compare the C++
version of the same function, which would return `-1` and rely on every caller
remembering to check.

The hidden case with all-negative values is there because a sentinel-shaped
implementation often initialises `best` to 0 and then reports no window at all
for data whose best sum is negative. `Option` forces the empty case to be
handled as a separate shape rather than as a suspicious value.

## The empty slice

`sum(&[])` is 0, with no special case, because the loop runs zero times. So
`n = 0` gives `whole 0`, `halves 0 0`, and two label-only lines - all of which
fall out of the code rather than needing a branch. An `n = 1` input gives an
empty left half for the same reason, since `1 / 2` is 0.

Empty is almost always the case that reveals whether a function was written in
terms of the data or in terms of assumptions about it.

## C++20's `std::span` is the same idea

```cpp
long long sum(std::span<const long long> xs);
```

Pointer plus length, no copy, accepts `std::vector`, `std::array` and C arrays.
What it does not have is the lifetime check: a `span` into a vector that is then
`push_back`ed is dangling, and nothing in the type system notices. It is the
right tool in modern C++ and it gives you the convenience without the
guarantee - which, by now, is a familiar shape of answer.
